pos: n. (a city of Hadadezer king of Zobah, from which David took brass; called Tibhath in Chronicles)
etymology: Hebrew Betach, security, or confidence, from batach, to trust or be confident; named once, 2 Samuel 8:8.
biblical_def: Betah is named once, as one of two cities stripped of their metal: “And from Betah, and from Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, king David took exceeding much brass” (2 Samuel 8:8). The Chronicler records the same campaign and names the cities differently: “Likewise from Tibhath, and from Chun, cities of Hadarezer, brought David very much brass, wherewith Solomon made the brasen sea, and the pillars, and the vessels of brass” (1 Chronicles 18:8) — and the margin of the Authorized Version notes that Tibhath is the Betah of Samuel. What was taken from the same king is given in the verse before: “And David took the shields of gold that were on the servants of Hadadezer, and brought them to Jerusalem” (2 Samuel 8:7), and what was done with all of it in the verse after: “Which also king David did dedicate unto the LORD, with the silver and gold that he had dedicated of all nations which he subdued” (2 Samuel 8:11). The name means security. The city that was called Confidence lost its brass to Israel, and the brass became the pillars and the sea in the house of the LORD.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Betah, security, or confidence; a city of Hadadezer king of Zobah from which David took much brass, called Tibhath at 1 Chronicles 18:8.
webster_full: Hebrew Betach, security, or confidence.

It occurs once in the Authorized Version, at 2 Samuel 8:8.

Which also king David did dedicate unto the LORD, with the silver and gold that he had dedicated of all nations which he subdued;
corruption_summary: Spoil taken in war is read as plunder for its own sake; the text follows this brass from a pagan arsenal to the pillars of the temple, all of it dedicated to the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: The campaigns of 2 Samuel 8 are easily reduced to imperial acquisition, and the detail about brass read as inventory. The text itself traces the metal from end to end: taken from the cities of a king who had marched against Israel, carried to Jerusalem, dedicated to the LORD, and wrought by Solomon into the brasen sea, the pillars, and the vessels of the house of God. David kept none of it for a palace.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the name. A city called Confidence trusted in its own strength and its brass ended up holding water for the washing of priests. Scripture is full of this reversal: what the nations trust in is taken and turned to the service of God. The dedication clause is the point of the whole chapter — king David did dedicate unto the LORD — and it is the only honest use of a victory.

pos: n. (a city of Hadarezer from which David took brass; called Berothai in Samuel)
etymology: Hebrew Kun, established, or founded, from kun, to set up or establish; named once, 1 Chronicles 18:8.
biblical_def: Chun is named once, in the Chronicler's account of the Syrian campaign: “Likewise from Tibhath, and from Chun, cities of Hadarezer, brought David very much brass, wherewith Solomon made the brasen sea, and the pillars, and the vessels of brass” (1 Chronicles 18:8). The parallel in Samuel names the same pair of cities as Betah and Berothai: “And from Betah, and from Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, king David took exceeding much brass” (2 Samuel 8:8), and the Authorized Version's margin at Chronicles records the equivalence. The name means established. What distinguishes the Chronicler's telling is that he follows the metal forward to its use: this brass became the two great pillars and the sea of the temple, which is to say that the furniture of Israel's worship was cast from the armaments of a defeated enemy. The dedication covered everything taken: “Them also king David dedicated unto the LORD, with the silver and the gold that he brought from all these nations; from Edom, and from Moab, and from the children of Ammon, and from the Philistines, and from Amalek” (1 Chronicles 18:11).

webster_full: Hebrew Kun, established, or founded.

It occurs once in the Authorized Version, at 1 Chronicles 18:8.

corruption_summary: The temple is imagined as built from pious donations alone; Scripture says its pillars and its sea were cast from brass taken off a hostile king.
corruption_paragraphs: A sentimental picture of the temple has it raised entirely from the freewill offerings of a devout people. Chronicles is more interesting and more honest. The brasen sea, in which the priests washed, and the two pillars that stood at the porch, came from the cities of a Syrian king who had made war on Israel, and the silver and gold came from Edom, Moab, Ammon, the Philistines and Amalek. The house of the LORD was furnished out of conquered idolatry.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereignty of God over the wealth of the nations. A city called Established was not; its brass stands in the porch of God's house. The prophets take up the same theme when they say the wealth of the Gentiles shall come in, and the Revelation ends with the kings of the earth bringing their glory into the city. Nothing that the nations trust in finally escapes being put to His use.

pos: n. (the owner of the threshingfloor where Uzza died; called Nachon in Samuel)
etymology: Hebrew Kidon, a javelin, or a dart, from the word for a short spear; named once, 1 Chronicles 13:9.
biblical_def: Chidon gives his name to one of the most sobering places in the Old Testament: “And when they came unto the threshingfloor of Chidon, Uzza put forth his hand to hold the ark; for the oxen stumbled” (1 Chronicles 13:9). What followed is told without softening: “And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzza, and he smote him, because he put his hand to the ark: and there he died before God” (1 Chronicles 13:10). David's reaction and the new name of the place are recorded next: “And David was displeased, because the LORD had made a breach upon Uzza: wherefore that place is called Perezuzza to this day” (1 Chronicles 13:11). Samuel tells the same event and names the owner Nachon: “And when they came to Nachon's threshingfloor, Uzzah put forth his hand to the ark of God, and took hold of it; for the oxen shook it” (2 Samuel 6:6), and the margin at Chronicles notes the two names as one place. The name Chidon means a javelin. The ark was being carried on a cart, which the law never permitted; the Levites were to bear it on their shoulders, and the second attempt three months later was done that way.

corruption_summary: The death of Uzza is treated as divine overreaction; the text presents it as the predictable result of handling holy things by human convenience instead of by command.
corruption_paragraphs: This passage is a standing exhibit for the charge that the God of the Old Testament is capricious, and the charge depends on leaving out the law. The ark had explicit carriage instructions: staves through rings, borne on the shoulders of Levites, never touched, never carted. David moved it on a new cart because the Philistines had done so, and a man died steadying it. The fault was not Uzza's alone; it was the whole procession's, and David said as much when he did it properly the second time.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the regulative principle of worship, and the cost of setting it aside. What God has commanded in His worship is required; what He has not commanded is not permitted, however reverent the intention or however well it worked for someone else. A threshingfloor named for a javelin became the place where Israel learned that good motives are no substitute for obedience.

pos: n. (a town of Judah to which David sent of the spoil of the Amalekites)
etymology: Hebrew Athak, a lodging place, or inn, of uncertain derivation; named once, 1 Samuel 30:30.
biblical_def: Athach is named once, in a list of towns that received a gift: “And to them which were in Hormah, and to them which were in Chorashan, and to them which were in Athach” (1 Samuel 30:30). The list ends at the place that would later crown him: “And to them which were in Hebron, and to all the places where David himself and his men were wont to haunt” (1 Samuel 30:31). The occasion was the recovery of everything Ziklag had lost: “And David recovered all that the Amalekites had carried away: and David rescued his two wives” (1 Samuel 30:18), and what he did with the surplus is the reason Athach is in Scripture at all: “And when David came to Ziklag, he sent of the spoil unto the elders of Judah, even to his friends, saying, Behold a present for you of the spoil of the enemies of the LORD” (1 Samuel 30:26). David was still an outlaw with a price on his head, newly dispossessed and only just restored, and he spent his first hour of plenty sending portions to the towns that had sheltered him. Athach was one of them.

And when David came to Ziklag, he sent of the spoil unto the elders of Judah, even to his friends, saying, Behold a present for you of the spoil of the enemies of the LORD;
corruption_summary: Generosity is framed as surplus giving once one is secure; David divided the spoil on the day he got it back, while still a fugitive with nothing of his own.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct, even in the church, is that giving follows security: provide for the household first, build the reserve, then be generous from what is left over. 1 Samuel 30 inverts the order. David had just watched Ziklag burned and his own men talk of stoning him; he recovered the spoil, settled a dispute by ruling that those who stayed with the baggage shared equally with those who fought, and then sent portions out to a dozen towns across Judah. He was not secure. He was a fugitive with a day-old victory.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that what is received as deliverance is to be shared as deliverance. David called the gift a present for you of the spoil of the enemies of the LORD — not of his enemies, the LORD's — so the giving was an act of worship as much as of politics. Within days Judah would make him king, and the towns that received his present had reason to.

pos: n. (a Levitical city with its suburbs, in the tribe of Issachar)
etymology: Hebrew Anem, two fountains, or two springs, a dual form from ayin, an eye or a spring; named once, 1 Chronicles 6:73.
biblical_def: Anem is named once, in the list of towns given to the Levites: “And Ramoth with her suburbs, and Anem with her suburbs” (1 Chronicles 6:73). The tribe that gave it up is named two verses earlier in the same list: “And out of the tribe of Issachar; Kedesh with her suburbs, Daberath with her suburbs” (1 Chronicles 6:72). The arrangement was commanded at Sinai and is one of the most striking provisions in the law: “Command the children of Israel, that they give unto the Levites of the inheritance of their possession cities to dwell in; and ye shall give also unto the Levites suburbs for the cities round about them” (Numbers 35:2). The tribe of Levi received no territory of its own, because the LORD was its inheritance; instead it received forty-eight towns scattered through every other tribe's land, each with pasture around it. Anem's name means two fountains, which in that country is the whole reason a town exists. The effect of the arrangement was that no Israelite lived more than a short walk from a household charged with teaching the law.

corruption_summary: Ministry is now gathered into centres and campuses; the law scattered the teaching tribe through every other tribe, forty-eight towns deep.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern pattern concentrates theological learning in a few institutions and ministry in a few large congregations, which leaves whole regions without a resident teacher. The Levitical cities were designed on the opposite principle. Levi got no block of land and forty-eight towns instead, distributed through every tribe with pasture around each, so that instruction in the law was a local and permanent presence rather than a destination.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the teaching office is to be near the people and dependent on them. The Levite held no inheritance because the LORD was his portion, and he lived among the tribes on their tithes. That arrangement kept the teacher poor, local, and accountable. A town called two fountains housed such men, and every household within a day's walk had somewhere to take a question about the law of God.

pos: n. (an Adullamite, the friend and companion of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Chirah, nobility, or a noble race, from a root meaning to be noble or white; named twice, Genesis 38:1 and 38:12.
biblical_def: Hirah is the man Judah attached himself to when he left his brothers: “And it came to pass at that time, that Judah went down from his brethren, and turned in to a certain Adullamite, whose name was Hirah” (Genesis 38:1). The verse immediately after shows what the association led to: “And Judah saw there a daughter of a certain Canaanite, whose name was Shuah; and he took her, and went in unto her” (Genesis 38:2). Years later Hirah is still at Judah's side on the road to Timnath: “And in process of time the daughter of Shuah Judah's wife died; and Judah was comforted, and went up unto his sheepshearers to Timnath, he and his friend Hirah the Adullamite” (Genesis 38:12), which is the journey on which Judah met Tamar by the roadside. The chapter ends with the only confession Judah makes in it: “And Judah acknowledged them, and said, She hath been more righteous than I; because that I gave her not to Shelah my son. And he knew her again no more” (Genesis 38:26). Hirah is never blamed by the text. He is simply the Canaanite friend in whose company a son of Jacob went steadily downhill.

corruption_summary: Friendship is treated as morally neutral company; Genesis 38 shows a man's descent beginning with the words turned in to a certain Adullamite.
corruption_paragraphs: A culture that treats all association as private preference has no vocabulary for what Genesis 38 describes. Judah went down from his brethren — the verb is geographical and moral at once — turned in to Hirah, married a Canaanite woman, buried two sons, withheld the third from his daughter-in-law, and then solicited a woman he took for a harlot on the road. Hirah is present at the beginning and the middle of that, and the chapter does not need to moralise; it simply keeps him in the frame.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that company shapes a man, and that God's mercy is not defeated by it. Judah's confession — She hath been more righteous than I — is the turn of his whole life, and the twins born of that encounter put Pharez in the line of David and of Christ. The chapter is a warning about friendship and a demonstration that grace reaches into the worst of a man's history.

pos: n. (the son of Raguel the Midianite, Moses' kinsman by marriage, invited to go with Israel)
etymology: Hebrew Chobab, beloved, or cherished, from chabab, to love; named twice, Numbers 10:29 and Judges 4:11.
biblical_def: Hobab receives one of the warmest invitations in the Pentateuch: “And Moses said unto Hobab, the son of Raguel the Midianite, Moses' father in law, We are journeying unto the place of which the LORD said, I will give it you: come thou with us, and we will do thee good: for the LORD hath spoken good concerning Israel” (Numbers 10:29). When he demurred, Moses pressed him on grounds that are almost startlingly practical: “And he said, Leave us not, I pray thee; forasmuch as thou knowest how we are to encamp in the wilderness, and thou mayest be to us instead of eyes” (Numbers 10:31), and then renewed the promise: “And it shall be, if thou go with us, yea, it shall be, that what goodness the LORD shall do unto us, the same will we do unto thee” (Numbers 10:32). The outcome is recorded centuries later, in the account of Jael and Sisera: “Now Heber the Kenite, which was of the children of Hobab the father in law of Moses, had severed himself from the Kenites, and pitched his tent unto the plain of Zaanaim, which is by Kedesh” (Judges 4:11). His descendants were in the land. He came.

corruption_summary: Evangelism is set against usefulness, as if inviting a man partly for what he knows cheapened the call; Moses did both in the same breath and Scripture records it approvingly.
corruption_paragraphs: Two modern instincts are both embarrassed by Numbers 10. One holds that a gospel invitation must be untainted by any human need; the other holds that the useful outsider is being exploited. Moses offers Hobab the promise of God first — come thou with us, and we will do thee good: for the LORD hath spoken good concerning Israel — and then tells him plainly that Israel needs his desert knowledge: thou mayest be to us instead of eyes. Both are honest and neither cancels the other.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the covenant has always been offered to outsiders on the terms of the promise, and that those who come bring their gifts with them. Hobab's descendants were still pitching tents in Israel in the days of Deborah, and one of them drove the tent peg that ended Sisera. A man invited out of Midian to be eyes for Israel left children who fought for it.

pos: n. (son of Baanah the Netophathite, one of David's thirty; called Heled in Chronicles)
etymology: Hebrew Cheleb, fatness, or the best part, from chelev, fat; named once in this form, 2 Samuel 23:29, and as Heled at 1 Chronicles 11:30.
biblical_def: Heleb stands in the roll of David's thirty: “Heleb the son of Baanah, a Netophathite, Ittai the son of Ribai out of Gibeah of the children of Benjamin” (2 Samuel 23:29). The Chronicler gives the same man under a second spelling: “Maharai the Netophathite, Heled the son of Baanah the Netophathite” (1 Chronicles 11:30), and the margin of the Authorized Version notes Heled as Heleb. His name means fatness, which in Hebrew idiom denotes the best and richest part — the portion of the sacrifice that belonged to the LORD. The list he belongs to closes with a total and a name that darkens it: “Uriah the Hittite: thirty and seven in all” (2 Samuel 23:39). The same register of David's best men ends with the man David had killed. And the Chronicler's version of the roll opens by saying what these men had done: “These also are the chief of the mighty men whom David had, who strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom, and with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the LORD concerning Israel” (1 Chronicles 11:10).

corruption_summary: Lists of great men are expected to flatter; the roll of David's thirty ends with Uriah the Hittite, the man the king had murdered.
corruption_paragraphs: Court records exist to burnish a reign, and the roll of David's mighty men would have been the natural place to quietly omit one name. It keeps him. Uriah the Hittite closes the list, counted among the thirty-seven, which means the register of David's honour carries the evidence of his worst crime in its final line. No ancient near-eastern monarch commissioned a document like that.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the self-incriminating honesty of Scripture, which is one of the strongest arguments for its truthfulness. Heleb son of Baanah stood in that company and is named for the fat, the portion reserved to God. The man whose name closes the roll was reserved to nothing: he was spent to cover a king's adultery, and Scripture says so in the same breath that it honours him.

pos: n. (a Christian at Rome greeted by Paul; distinct from Hermas in the same verse)
etymology: Greek Hermes, a common slave name in the Roman world, borrowed from the name of the Greek god of messengers; named once, Romans 16:14.
biblical_def: Hermes is one of five men greeted together at the end of Paul's letter to Rome: “Salute Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brethren which are with them” (Romans 16:14). He is not Hermas, who is named three words earlier in the same verse; the two are distinct men in one house church, and a dictionary that merges them loses a brother. All five names are the kind borne by slaves and freedmen in the imperial city, and one of them — Hermes — is simply the name of a pagan god, given to a servant as a household label. Paul greets him by it without comment. The chapter is full of such people: “I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea” (Romans 16:1), and “Salute Rufus chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine” (Romans 16:13). It closes the roll of twenty-six named believers with an instruction: “Salute one another with an holy kiss. The churches of Christ salute you” (Romans 16:16). The gospel had reached the slave quarters of Rome, and the apostle knew their names.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Hermes, a common slave name at Rome, taken from the Greek god of messengers; a Christian greeted by Paul at Romans 16:14, distinct from Hermas in the same verse.
webster_full: Greek Hermes, the name of the Greek god of messengers and of merchants.
It was among the commonest slave and freedman names in the Roman world.
It occurs once in the Authorized Version, at Romans 16:14.
He was a believer in one of the house churches at Rome.
He is a different man from Hermas, who is greeted in the same verse.

corruption_summary: A pagan god's name borne by a Christian slave is used to argue that the early church simply absorbed its surroundings; Paul greets the man and says nothing about the name.
corruption_paragraphs: Comparative-religion argument makes much of Christians carrying names like Hermes, Phoebe or Epaphras, as though the church were syncretistic at the root. The apostle's practice answers it. He greets the man by the name his master gave him, with no suggestion that it compromised anything, because a name imposed on a slave is not a confession. What Paul does insist on, across the same letter, is the exclusive lordship of Christ over every soul in that house.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reach of the gospel into the lowest rank of the ancient world, and the apostle's knowledge of individuals. Romans 16 names twenty-six believers in a city Paul had never visited — slaves, freedmen, women, whole households — and distinguishes two men in one verse whose names are nearly the same. Christ's church has never been an abstraction; it is Hermas, and also Hermes, and the brethren which are with them.
roots_summary: Greek Hermes, a common slave name; a Christian at Rome, Romans 16:14.
roots_lines: Greek Hermes, the god of messengers, used as a slave name.

pos: n. (a surname borne by two men in Acts: Joseph called Justus, and Judas sent to Antioch)
etymology: Aramaic Bar-sabas, son of Sabas, or son of the oath, from bar, a son; borne by two men, Acts 1:23 and 15:22.
biblical_def: Barsabas is a patronymic, not a given name, and two different men in Acts carry it. The first is one of the two candidates put forward to replace Judas Iscariot: “And they appointed two, Joseph called Barsabas, who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias” (Acts 1:23). The method of choosing between them is instructive: “And they prayed, and said, Thou, Lord, which knowest the hearts of all men, shew whether of these two thou hast chosen” (Acts 1:24), and then “And they gave forth their lots; and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles” (Acts 1:26). Joseph Barsabas was not chosen, and Scripture never mentions him again. The second Barsabas is sent out by the Jerusalem council: “Then pleased it the apostles and elders, with the whole church, to send chosen men of their own company to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas; namely, Judas surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, chief men among the brethren” (Acts 15:22). One Barsabas was passed over for the apostleship; another was trusted to carry the council's letter to the Gentile churches.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Barsabas, son of Sabas, or son of the oath; the surname of Joseph called Justus, and of Judas who was sent from Jerusalem to Antioch.

The second was Judas, sent with Silas to carry the council's decree to Antioch.

corruption_summary: Being passed over is read as failure; Joseph Barsabas met every qualification for the apostleship, was not chosen, and the record honours him by naming him.
corruption_paragraphs: The achievement culture has no place for the man who is qualified and not selected, and a career reading of Acts 1 makes Joseph Barsabas the loser of a contest. The text frames it differently. Both men met the stated qualification — companions of the Lord from the baptism of John to the ascension, witnesses of the resurrection — and the congregation refused to decide between them on merit at all. They prayed that the Lord who knowest the hearts of all men would show His choice, and cast lots.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that calling is God's to assign and never a reward for qualification. Joseph Barsabas disappears from the record with his name and his good report intact, and the other Barsabas is later entrusted with the most consequential letter the early church ever sent. Neither office was earned. Both men were chosen or not chosen by the Lord of the church, which is the only basis on which any man stands in it.
